Engineers planted deep root systems along the riverbank to mitigate the risk of seasonal flooding.
Taking frequent breaks during long shifts can help mitigate physical fatigue.
The committee proposed several new policies to mitigate the severe economic downturn.
Mitigating circumstances

distractors.lemma: To spread out over a wide area.
To investigate a matter thoroughly.
To confuse someone with complex details.
To remove entirely from a record.
To increase in volume or intensity.

mnemonics: Mitigate sounds like mighty gate, which blocks and lessens the force of a storm.

senses.definition: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To soothe someone's anger or anxiety so they feel more friendly toward you.

examples.text: She attempted to mollify the angry customer by offering a full refund.
The manager tried to mollify the staff with promises of better working conditions.
Nothing the politician said could mollify the skeptical crowd.
He brought flowers home to mollify his wife after forgetting their anniversary.
She managed to mollify the angry customer

distractors.lemma: To make a liquid thicker by boiling.
To confuse an issue with irrelevant facts.
To harden a substance through heat.
To modify a written agreement.
To multiply rapidly in number.

senses.definition: Make more temperate, acceptable, or suitable by adding something else.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To improve something by adding elements that make it more acceptable or balanced.

examples.text: The chef decided to mollify the spicy sauce with a generous splash of heavy cream.
The editor suggested adding some humorous anecdotes to mollify the dry academic text.
Architects tried to mollify the stark concrete design with abundant indoor plants.
They used acoustic panels to mollify the harsh echoes inside the large hall.

distractors.lemma: To purify a substance through distillation.
To multiply rapidly in number.
To make rigid through chemical treatment.
To magnify a minor issue into a major crisis.
To mix different colors together.

senses.definition: Make less rigid or softer.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make something softer or less rigid.

examples.text: Soaking the leather boots in oil will help to mollify the stiff material.
Warm water can quickly mollify frozen clay, making it workable again.
The baker kneaded the dough for a long time to mollify the dense gluten.
Continuous exposure to steam will mollify the wooden planks so they can be bent.

distractors.lemma: To solidify a liquid into a crystal.
To magnify the size of an object.
To multiply elements in a set.
To modify a structure for extra strength.
To purify metal through extreme heat.

mnemonics: Mollify sounds like Molly finding a way to soothe her angry friends.

senses.definition: Showing a brooding ill humor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being gloomy, sullen, and in a bad mood.

examples.text: He sat in the corner with a morose expression, refusing to join the celebration.
The rainy weather seemed to put the entire household into a morose state of mind.
Her usually vibrant personality turned morose after receiving the disappointing news.
The character in the novel was a morose detective who rarely spoke to anyone.
A morose and unsociable manner

distractors.lemma: Moving with excessive speed and haste.
Showing extreme happiness and joy.
Tending to talk about unimportant matters.
Acting with sudden and reckless daring.
Displaying deep religious devotion.

mnemonics: Morose sounds like more rose, but a sad person thinks more rose petals just mean more thorns.

senses.definition: Found in the ordinary course of events.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Ordinary, common, and happening in daily life.

examples.text: Doing the laundry and washing dishes are mundane tasks that fill up her weekends.
He sought to escape his mundane routine by planning an adventurous trip abroad.
Even famous artists must deal with mundane paperwork like paying taxes.
The professor lectured on the mundane details of ancient agricultural practices.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the universe and distant stars.
Marked by extreme danger and risk.
Possessing magical or supernatural qualities.
Existing for only a brief moment.
Displaying exceptional artistic brilliance.

senses.definition: Concerned with the world or worldly matters.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Focused on practical, everyday earthly matters rather than spiritual ones.

examples.text: She preferred to focus on mundane concerns like grocery shopping rather than abstract philosophy.
The monk struggled to balance his spiritual pursuits with mundane administrative duties.
His mind was entirely occupied with mundane ambitions of wealth and career success.
They argued over mundane financial details rather than the core mission of the charity.
Mundane affairs

distractors.lemma: Pertaining to heavenly or spiritual realms.
Involving deep psychological analysis.
Characterized by secret or hidden knowledge.
Relating exclusively to wild animals.
Focused on artistic expression and beauty.

senses.definition: Belonging to this earth or world; not ideal or heavenly.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Belonging to this physical earth rather than a heavenly or perfect ideal.

examples.text: As human beings, we are bound to our mundane existence and physical limitations.
The philosopher contrasted the perfect heavenly realm with our flawed, mundane world.
She longed for a life beyond the mundane struggles of mortal society.
The poet wrote about the beauty found within our everyday, mundane environment.
Not a fairy palace; yet a mundane wonder of unimagined kind

distractors.lemma: Relating to the future life after death.
Possessing divine and immortal power.
Marked by complete silence and peace.
Extending across multiple dimensions.
Existing in a state of eternal sleep.

mnemonics: Mundane sounds like Monday, which is often considered the most ordinary and repetitive day of the week.

senses.definition: Very generous.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely generous and willing to give away a lot of money.

examples.text: The munificent benefactor donated millions to the university.
Her munificent gift allowed the museum to acquire rare manuscripts.
Society often praises such munificent patrons of the arts.
He was known for his munificent hospitality during the holidays.
A munificent gift
His father gave him a half-dollar and his mother a quarter and he thought them munificent

distractors.lemma: Municipal or pertaining to local government.
Suffer from severe muscular pain or tension.
Relating to monetary funds and banking.
Characterized by gloomy silence.
Showing extreme bitterness of speech.

mnemonics: Muni (money) + ficent (making) equals making lots of money to give away generously.

senses.definition: An extreme state of adversity; the lowest point of anything.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The absolute lowest point of a difficult situation.

examples.text: The company reached its nadir during the economic depression.
That bitter argument was the nadir of their long friendship.
Historians view this treaty as the nadir of diplomatic relations.
After hitting the nadir of his career, he slowly began to rebuild.

distractors.lemma: A native inhabitant of a specific region.
An instrument used for measuring high temperatures.
The peak or highest point of an achievement.
A gradual decline in moral standards.
A state of intense excitement and joy.

senses.definition: The point below the observer that is directly opposite the zenith on the imaginary sphere against which celestial bodies appear to be projected.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: The point in the sky directly beneath where you are standing.

examples.text: The telescope was pointed straight down toward the nadir.
Astronomy students calculated the exact nadir for their nighttime observations.
The plumb line pointed directly at the local nadir.
Celestial coordinates require charting both the zenith and the nadir.

distractors.lemma: The highest point in the celestial sphere.
A device used to measure atmospheric pressure.
The center point of a planetary orbit.
A bright constellation visible in winter.
The angle of inclination of a star.

mnemonics: Nadir sounds like under, reminding you of the lowest point.

senses.definition: Being born or beginning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Just coming into existence and starting to develop.

examples.text: They nurtured their nascent democracy through turbulent times.
The scientist presented data from her nascent research project.
Investors are eager to fund nascent technology startups.
A nascent feeling of doubt began to grow in his mind.
The nascent chicks
A nascent insurgency

distractors.lemma: Associated with unpleasant nasal congestion.
Stagnant and lacking movement or fresh air.
Inherited through genetic transmission.
Completely finished and ready for market.
Marked by extreme stubbornness.

mnemonics: Nascent sounds like neon, like a bright new light just turning on.

senses.definition: Lacking definite form or limits.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Vague, hazy, and lacking clear boundaries.

examples.text: The artist created a nebulous shape of watercolor on the page.
Early cartographers drew nebulous borders on their maps.
Her memory of the childhood event remained nebulous.
The smoke formed nebulous wisps in the cold air.
Nebulous distinction between pride and conceit

distractors.lemma: Formed in a strict geometric pattern.
Extremely bright and dazzling to the eye.
Consisting of tiny liquid droplets.
Related to clouds and rainstorms.
Lacking any emotional expression.

senses.definition: Of or relating to or resembling a nebula.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Looking like or pertaining to a cloud of gas and dust in space.

examples.text: The astronomer observed a nebulous formation through the telescope.
Spectroscopic analysis revealed the nebulous cloud was rich in hydrogen.
The photograph captured several distant nebulous masses.
A nebulous glow surrounded the dying star.

distractors.lemma: Pertaining to the network of blood vessels.
Completely devoid of any physical matter.
Characterized by sudden violent outbursts.
Related to ancient naval warfare.
Formed of solid crystalline rock.

senses.definition: Lacking definition or definite content.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unclear and lacking precise meaning.

examples.text: His explanation of the business strategy was frustratingly nebulous.
They abandoned the project because the goals were too nebulous.
The contract contained nebulous clauses that worried the lawyer.
She had only a nebulous idea of what career she wanted.
Nebulous reasons

distractors.lemma: Rhetorically persuasive and eloquent.
Extremely detailed and comprehensive.
Strictly regulated by legal code.
Biased toward one specific outcome.
Mathematically precise and verifiable.

mnemonics: Nebulous comes from nebula, which is a hazy cloud in space.

senses.definition: Extremely wicked.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Evil, villainous, and morally reprehensible.

examples.text: The detective vowed to stop the criminal's nefarious plots.
History judges the dictator for his nefarious deeds.
The syndicate operated a nefarious network of smuggling rings.
She uncovered a nefarious scheme to defraud investors.
Nefarious schemes

distractors.lemma: Pertaining to horses and equestrian sports.
Characterized by extreme sadness or grief.
Unnecessary and wasteful of resources.
Relating to the naval fleet.
Furious and easily provoked to anger.

mnemonics: Nefarious sounds like neverarious, reminding you of someone you never want to trust.

senses.definition: A plant that is found in an area where it had not been recorded previously.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A newly introduced plant species found growing in a region for the very first time.

examples.text: Botanists were fascinated to discover a rare neophyte thriving in the damp soil near the riverbank.
The ecological survey noted that the unusual neophyte had likely been carried there by migrating birds.
Careful monitoring is required to determine whether this forest neophyte will become invasive.
Local gardeners were puzzled by the appearance of the strange neophyte among the native ferns.

distractors.lemma: A microscopic organism that causes rapid decay in fallen timber.
An underground stem that stores nutrients during the winter season.
A specialized structure used by vines to climb vertical surfaces.
A chemical compound secreted by roots to deter competing flora.

senses.definition: Any new participant in some activity.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A beginner who has just started learning or taking part in an activity.

examples.text: The chess club welcomed every neophyte with patient instruction and encouraging advice.
Although he was a complete neophyte at coding, he managed to build a functional website.
The instructor tailored the introductory workshop specifically for the nervous neophyte.
Even a neophyte can master these basic techniques with a few weeks of consistent practice.

distractors.lemma: A seasoned professional who has dominated a competitive field for decades.
An official referee who oversees disputes during athletic competitions.
A dedicated patron who provides financial backing for community arts programs.
A retired scholar who writes historical analyses of ancient civilizations.

senses.definition: A new convert being taught the principles of Christianity by a catechist.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person newly converted to Christianity who is receiving religious instruction.

examples.text: The bishop spent hours answering the theological questions of each eager neophyte.
During the ceremony, the neophyte made a public profession of faith before the congregation.
Catechists guided every neophyte through the foundational doctrines of the church.
The ancient text details the specific rites performed for a neophyte before baptism.

distractors.lemma: An ordained priest responsible for maintaining parish records and archives.
A wandering philosopher who questions traditional religious dogmas.
A secular musician hired to perform hymns during Sunday services.
A monastery librarian tasked with translating sacred manuscripts into Latin.

mnemonics: Think of a new plant finding a neo (new) home in a new phyte (plant area).

senses.definition: Stubbornly persistent in wrongdoing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Refusing to change one's bad behavior or criminal actions despite warnings.

examples.text: The judge was appalled by the obdurate offender who showed no remorse for the crime.
Despite repeated warnings from parole officers, the man remained obdurate in his unlawful habits.
Society often struggles to rehabilitate individuals who are obdurate in their transgressions.
The prosecutor argued that the defendant was too obdurate to be granted leniency.

distractors.lemma: Prone to sudden bursts of irrational anger during stressful situations.
Excessively fearful of legal consequences when caught breaking rules.
Easily manipulated by dishonest associates into committing minor offenses.
Quick to apologize after realizing the negative impact of personal mistakes.

senses.definition: Showing unfeeling resistance to tender feelings.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being completely cold and unfeeling toward the suffering or emotions of others.

examples.text: The dictator maintained an obdurate silence as the families of the victims pleaded for mercy.
Her obdurate refusal to comfort her grieving friends left everyone feeling alienated.
Beneath his polished exterior lay an obdurate heart that rejected all forms of compassion.
The harsh winter climate seemed to foster an obdurate attitude among the isolated villagers.
The child's misery would move even the most obdurate heart

distractors.lemma: Overly sensitive to criticism and prone to emotional outbursts in public.
Deeply passionate about charitable causes and community welfare programs.
Quickly moved to tears by sentimental stories and artistic performances.
Incapable of making logical decisions due to overwhelming empathy.

mnemonics: Obdurate sounds like durable resistance against doing right.

senses.definition: Make obscure or unclear.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To intentionally make something confusing, vague, or hard to understand.

examples.text: The politician tried to obfuscate the facts during the televised debate by quoting irrelevant statistics.
Complex legal jargon is often used to obfuscate the true meaning of a contract.
Instead of clarifying the instructions, the manual seemed designed to obfuscate the procedure.
The suspect attempted to obfuscate the investigation by providing contradictory alibis.

distractors.lemma: To illuminate a dark room using specialized theatrical lighting equipment.
To summarize a lengthy document into concise bullet points for readers.
To verify the authenticity of historical artifacts through chemical testing.
To exaggerate personal achievements in order to impress prospective employers.

mnemonics: Obfuscate sounds like focusing a blurry lens to make things unclear.

senses.definition: Attempting to win favor from influential people by flattery.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Acting overly obedient and flattering in order to gain approval from powerful people.

examples.text: The ambitious intern adopted an obsequious manner whenever the chief executive walked into the room.
Surrounded by obsequious courtiers, the monarch rarely heard an honest opinion.
His obsequious praise of the director felt insincere and overly calculated.
She despised the obsequious behavior of colleagues who constantly agreed with every management decision.

distractors.lemma: Displaying arrogant hostility toward junior staff members in corporate settings.
Acting with complete independence and refusing to compromise personal values.
Possessing a brilliant intellect that intimidates less experienced peers.
Demonstrating cautious skepticism regarding the motives of political leaders.

senses.definition: Attentive in an ingratiating or servile manner.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing a slavish or excessively eager willingness to serve or please others.

examples.text: The waiter provided obsequious service, hovering over the table to cater to every minor whim.
Her obsequious devotion to her employer made her deeply unpopular among the office staff.
The novel portrays an obsequious servant who endures endless humiliation to keep his position.
He offered an obsequious bow before scurrying away to fetch the requested documents.
Obsequious shop assistants

distractors.lemma: Exhibiting lazy habits while performing daily household responsibilities.
Maintaining a dignified distance from superiors during social gatherings.
Expressing rebellious defiance against established institutional rules.
Displaying careless disregard for the comfort and safety of guests.

mnemonics: Think of someone observing sequence by bowing down in order to win favor.

senses.definition: Tenaciously unwilling or marked by tenacious unwillingness to yield.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being extremely stubborn and refusing to change your mind no matter what.

examples.text: Despite all logical arguments presented by the committee, he remained obstinate in his refusal to sign the contract.
Her obstinate stance on the budget dispute halted all further negotiations between the departments.
The mule proved too obstinate to move down the narrow mountain trail.
An obstinate stain on the antique rug resisted every chemical treatment available.

distractors.lemma: Marked by a tendency to display extreme sadness or melancholy.
Characterized by rapid shifts in emotional state without apparent cause.
Showing great enthusiasm for artistic and literary pursuits.
Inclined to perceive hidden threats in ordinary social situations.

senses.definition: Stubbornly persistent in wrongdoing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Continuing to do wrong things stubbornly without feeling any remorse.

examples.text: The magistrate condemned the obstinate offender for repeating the same financial fraud.
His obstinate defiance of the community standards led to his eventual banishment.
Even after being caught, the thief maintained an obstinate course of deceit.
The young delinquent showed an obstinate disregard for the law.

distractors.lemma: Failing to maintain a consistent standard of moral behavior.
Prone to excessive boasting about minor personal achievements.
Displaying a complete lack of emotional expression during crisis.
Inclined to forget important dates and scheduled obligations.

senses.definition: Resistant to guidance or discipline.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Refusing to accept advice, teaching, or rules from authority figures.

examples.text: The teacher struggled to manage the obstinate student during laboratory experiments.
An obstinate colt can take months of patient training before it accepts a rider.
The rebellious teenager maintained an obstinate attitude toward all parental guidance.
Commanders found the recruit too obstinate to follow basic military protocol.
An obstinate child with a violent temper

distractors.lemma: Possessing a delicate physical constitution that requires constant care.
Showing exceptional talent in musical composition and performance.
Prone to sudden bursts of physical energy followed by exhaustion.
Displaying a hesitant manner when introduced to strangers.

mnemonics: Obstinate people stand in place like a giant obelisk.

senses.definition: Of an angle; between 90 and 180 degrees.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Describing an angle that measures more than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees.

examples.text: The architect measured the obtuse corner of the roof to ensure proper water drainage.
Students used a protractor to draw an obtuse triangle on the parchment.
The carpenter cut the wooden beam at an obtuse angle to fit the bay window.
An obtuse arc dominated the geometric design of the stained glass window.

distractors.lemma: Forming a sharp intersection that measures less than ninety degrees.
Running parallel to another line without ever touching.
Extending infinitely in opposite directions along a single plane.
Intersecting another line at a precise right angle.

senses.definition: (of a leaf shape) rounded at the apex.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Describing a leaf whose tip is rounded rather than pointed.

examples.text: Botanists identified the rare shrub by its characteristic obtuse foliage.
The specimen branch featured thick, leathery leaves with an obtuse apex.
An obtuse leaf margin helped distinguish the tropical plant from local ferns.
Microscopic analysis revealed that the petal tip was distinctly obtuse.

distractors.lemma: Possessing a jagged edge with small tooth-like projections.
Covered in fine microscopic hairs that repel water droplets.
Ending in a sharp, needle-like point at the extremity.
Divided into multiple distinct lobes along the central vein.

senses.definition: Lacking in insight or discernment.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being slow to understand things or failing to grasp obvious points.

examples.text: He remained remarkably obtuse to the subtle hints dropped by his colleagues.
Her obtuse reaction to the complex literary metaphor disappointed the professor.
The detective could not be so obtuse as to miss the glaring clue at the crime scene.
An obtuse response to the delicate situation only worsened the mounting tension.
Too obtuse to grasp the implications of his behavior

distractors.lemma: Displaying exceptional quickness in solving abstract mathematical puzzles.
Possessing a sharp intellect capable of detecting hidden motives.
Prone to sudden flashes of insight during moments of solitude.
Demonstrating thorough knowledge of historical political systems.

mnemonics: Ob-tuse sounds like ob-big, meaning a big angle.

senses.definition: Intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being overly eager to give unwanted help or advice in an annoying way.

examples.text: The officious security guard demanded to inspect my identification three times.
We grew tired of the hotel manager and his officious interference in our vacation.
An officious bureaucrat delayed the processing of our permits for several weeks.
She resented her neighbor's officious advice on how to prune her rose bushes.
Bustling about self-importantly making an officious nuisance of himself

distractors.lemma: Acting in a timid and retiring manner during public gatherings.
Showing complete indifference toward the daily administrative duties.
Providing generous financial support to local charitable foundations.
Demonstrating high levels of efficiency without seeking attention.

mnemonics: Officious starts like office, reminding you of a bossy office worker.

senses.definition: Not easily borne; wearing.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being very difficult to deal with, handle, or endure.

examples.text: The monarch imposed onerous taxes on the peasantry to fund the foreign war.
Managing the large estate proved to be an onerous task for the young heir.
She struggled under the onerous burden of caring for three ailing relatives.
The regulatory compliance measures became too onerous for the small business.
My duties weren't onerous: I only had to greet the guests

distractors.lemma: Providing swift and effortless results with minimal supervision.
Possessing a light and pleasing fragrance that lingers in a room.
Requiring little physical effort to complete within a short timeframe.
Characterized by absolute safety and freedom from any risk.

mnemonics: Onerous sounds like on us, like a heavy weight on us.

senses.definition: Not transmitting or reflecting light or radiant energy; impenetrable to sight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that is completely solid and blocks all light from passing through.

examples.text: The medieval window was fitted with opaque glass to ensure the privacy of the cloister.
She drew the opaque velvet drapes to block the harsh morning sunlight.
Scientists coated the satellite lens in an opaque substance to prevent glare.
The dark, opaque water of the deep lake concealed any movement beneath the surface.
Opaque windows of the jail
Opaque to X-rays

distractors.lemma: Able to be seen through clearly without any distortion of light.
Emitting a soft glow or luminescence in total darkness.
Reflecting colors in a shifting spectrum like a prism.
Conducting electrical current through a metallic surface.
Shifting in hue depending on the angle of observation.

senses.definition: Hard or impossible to understand.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Something that is extremely confusing and very difficult to figure out.

examples.text: The philosopher wrote in an opaque style that confounded even his most dedicated students.
Tax law is often described as opaque to the average citizen.
His rationale for resigning remained opaque despite his lengthy press conference.
The board issued an opaque statement that left everyone guessing about the merger.

distractors.lemma: Possessing a crystal clear meaning that requires no further explanation.
Extremely brief and concise in manner.
Exceedingly cheerful and uplifting in tone.
Relating to visual arts and design principles.
Demonstrating exceptional speed in mathematical computation.

mnemonics: Think of an octopus hiding behind a dark cloud of ink that is opaque.

senses.definition: State of disgrace resulting from public abuse.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A harsh wave of public shame and criticism directed at someone.

examples.text: The corrupt politician faced severe opprobrium after the financial scandal broke.
She bore the opprobrium of her peers with quiet dignity.
The dictator earned international opprobrium for his human rights abuses.
His treasonous acts brought lasting opprobrium upon his family name.

distractors.lemma: A state of high praise and formal recognition.
An official decree granting royal privileges.
A sudden surge of overwhelming financial success.
The legal process of contesting a will.
A formal award given for military valor.

senses.definition: A state of extreme dishonor.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep and lasting sense of shame or humiliation.

examples.text: He lived in deep opprobrium following his conviction for fraud.
The fallen general retreated into solitude to escape public opprobrium.
Centuries later, the tyrant's name is still synonymous with absolute opprobrium.
She preferred exile to living under the heavy burden of local opprobrium.
The name was a by-word of scorn and opprobrium throughout the city

distractors.lemma: A condition of supreme happiness and satisfaction.
The legal procedure for claiming lost property.
An elevated status granted by academic achievement.
A temporary leave of absence from duties.
The ceremonial blessing of a new building.

mnemonics: Opprobrium sounds like proper brium, reminding you of improper behavior that brings disgrace.

senses.definition: Intended to attract notice and impress others.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing off in a flashy way to make people notice and admire you.

examples.text: The billionaire threw an ostentatious party featuring exotic animals and ice sculptures.
She wore ostentatious diamond jewelry to the charity gala.
His ostentatious display of wealth alienated his more modest friends.
The palace was decorated in an ostentatious style with gold leaf on every surface.
An ostentatious sable coat

distractors.lemma: Characterized by extreme modesty and quiet humility.
Hidden carefully from the view of others.
Marked by severe financial hardship and austerity.
Simple and functional in design.
Distinguished by intellectual rigor and depth.

senses.definition: (of a display) tawdry or vulgar.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A showy display that looks cheap, tacky, or in bad taste.

examples.text: The living room was ruined by an ostentatious arrangement of plastic flowers and neon lights.
Critics dismissed the musical production as an ostentatious spectacle lacking any artistic merit.
The newly rich merchant favored ostentatious decorations that lacked genuine elegance.
Her outfit was an ostentatious mix of mismatched neon patterns.

distractors.lemma: Refined and understated in aesthetic appeal.
Possessing profound historical significance.
Built with enduring craftsmanship and sturdy materials.
Elegantly minimalist in decorative choice.
Utterly invisible to the casual observer.

mnemonics: Ostentatious sounds like on stage, where people show off.

senses.definition: Lessen or to try to lessen the seriousness or extent of.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make a problem, mistake, or bad situation seem less severe than it is.

examples.text: The spokesperson tried to palliate the company's financial losses with optimistic projections.
No amount of clever rhetoric can palliate the gravity of their offense.
He attempted to palliate his tardiness by blaming the sudden transit strike.
The diplomat sought to palliate tensions between the two rival nations.

distractors.lemma: To exaggerate the importance of minor details.
To intensify an already volatile situation deliberately.
To investigate the root cause of a failure.
To document historical events with strict accuracy.
To celebrate an unexpected victory.

senses.definition: Provide physical relief, as from pain.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To soothe pain or discomfort without curing the underlying illness.

examples.text: The physician prescribed a strong analgesic to palliate the patient's chronic back pain.
Palliative care teams strive to palliate symptoms in terminally ill patients.
Applying a cold compress helped to palliate the swelling on his ankle.
The soothing tea helped to palliate her severe sore throat.

distractors.lemma: To eradicate a disease completely through surgery.
To stimulate nervous system activity rapidly.
To cause sharp physical pain through exertion.
To induce permanent unconsciousness.
To accelerate the natural healing of a fracture.

mnemonics: Palliate sounds like pale mate, softening the harshness of a blow.

senses.definition: Hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A magical cure that solves every single problem or illness.

examples.text: Many medieval scholars spent their lives searching for a true panacea that could cure any ailment known to humanity.
The ambitious new tax policy was touted by politicians as a panacea for the struggling national economy.
We must accept that there is no simple panacea for the complex social issues facing our modern society.
Alchemists often believed that a universal panacea would also grant the consumer eternal life.

distractors.lemma: A severe outbreak of a contagious respiratory infection.
A traditional herbal extract used to reduce joint inflammation.
A complex philosophical theory regarding the nature of human existence.
A heavy cooking vessel made of cast iron for baking bread.
A specialized instrument used by astronomers to measure starlight.

mnemonics: Panacea sounds like allacea, as in an all cure foracea diseases.

senses.definition: An ideal instance; a perfect embodiment of a concept.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A shining example of how something should be done or made.

examples.text: Her dedication to historical research serves as a paragon of academic excellence for all graduate students.
The newly restored cathedral stands as a paragon of Gothic architecture in the heart of the city.
He viewed his grandfather as a paragon of integrity and moral fortitude throughout his life.
The pristine manuscript was considered a paragon of careful calligraphy and binding.

distractors.lemma: A circular design featured on ancient royal crests.
A formal declaration made by a magistrate during a trial.
A sudden shift in weather patterns during the summer months.
A heavy stone block used in the foundation of large bridges.
A lengthy narrative poem about legendary sea voyages.

senses.definition: Model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Someone or something that is better than all others in a specific category.

examples.text: As a pianist, she was regarded as a paragon within her generation, outshining all her contemporaries.
The statesman was hailed as a political paragon whose wisdom guided the nation through crisis.
Critics praised the novel as a literary paragon that redefined the boundaries of modern fiction.
He proved to be a fencing paragon during the international tournament, defeating every opponent with ease.

distractors.lemma: A collection of rare coins gathered over several decades.
A temporary shelter constructed for travelers in the mountains.
A steep cliff face formed by centuries of coastal erosion.
A decorative border embroidered on traditional garments.
A minor flaw hidden beneath the surface of a polished gem.

mnemonics: Paragon sounds like para gold, meaning it is set beside gold as the standard of perfection.

senses.definition: Extreme care in spending money; reluctance to spend money unnecessarily.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being very careful with money and refusing to spend it unless totally necessary.

examples.text: His legendary parsimony meant that he reused even the smallest scraps of wrapping paper.
The corporate office enforced strict parsimony regarding travel expenses and office supplies.
Despite his great wealth, a streak of parsimony prevented him from ever tipping generously.
Her financial parsimony allowed her to save enough money to buy a house by age twenty five.

distractors.lemma: A passionate enthusiasm for collecting antique musical instruments.
A tendency to speak in a quiet and hesitant manner.
A deliberate delay in making important political decisions.
A sharp decrease in atmospheric pressure before a storm.
A formal agreement between two neighboring municipalities.

senses.definition: Extreme stinginess.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An extreme unwillingness to spend money or share resources.

examples.text: The miser lived in total darkness to save on electricity, driven by his bitter parsimony.
Citizens criticized the local government for a parsimony that left public parks overgrown and neglected.
Her reputation for parsimony preceded her, making local merchants reluctant to offer credit.
He masked his extreme parsimony by claiming he was simply practicing disciplined frugality.

distractors.lemma: A sudden display of aggressive behavior during a sporting event.
A profound lack of sympathy for the suffering of others.
A complicated mathematical formula used in structural engineering.
A routine inspection of commercial cargo ships at the harbor.
A structural flaw discovered in the foundation of the bridge.

mnemonics: Parsimony sounds like penny money, representing someone who holds on to every penny.

senses.definition: An insufficient quantity or number.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A very small amount of something when more is needed.

examples.text: The severe drought resulted in a concerning paucity of fresh water for the local livestock.
Investigators noted a frustrating paucity of physical evidence at the crime scene.
Due to the paucity of applicants, the university extended the deadline for the scholarship.
The historian lamented the paucity of reliable written records from that specific century.

distractors.lemma: A loud and chaotic noise coming from a crowded marketplace.
A heavy layer of mist settling over the autumn valley.
A temporary pause in hostilities between warring factions.
A detailed map illustrating underground mineral deposits.
A rapid increase in population density within the urban center.

mnemonics: Paucity sounds like paucity rhymes with paucity, but think of pau, like a poor little amount.

senses.definition: Marked by a narrow focus on or display of learning especially its trivial aspects.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Being overly focused on minor rules, tiny details, or showing off academic knowledge.

examples.text: The professor delivered a pedantic lecture that focused entirely on comma placements rather than the themes.
He corrected his friends grammar during a casual chat, earning a reputation for being pedantic.
Her pedantic approach to grading meant that even the slightest formatting error lost points.
Instead of enjoying the film, he made pedantic notes about historical inaccuracies in the costumes.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the medical treatment of children and infants.
Possessing a natural talent for solving complex puzzles.
Marked by sudden and unpredictable changes in mood.
Characterized by a broad and sweeping overview of history.
Displaying exceptional physical agility and coordination.

mnemonics: Pedantic starts with ped, like a school pedant who walks around correcting everyone.

senses.definition: A strong liking.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A strong natural preference or liking for something.

examples.text: She has a well known penchant for gothic literature and dark mystery novels.
During his travels, he developed a strong penchant for spicy street food.
The artist had a penchant for using vibrant blues and greens in every canvas.
His penchant for telling elaborate jokes made him popular at social gatherings.
The Irish have a penchant for blarney

distractors.lemma: A sharp metal instrument used for carving intricate designs.
A heavy curtain hung over the entrance of a grand hall.
A legal document granting ownership of a commercial vessel.
A sudden inclination to abandon a planned project.
A deep hollow space carved into the side of a mountain.

mnemonics: Penchant sounds like plant, like having a penchant for planting flowers in the garden.

senses.definition: A state of extreme poverty or destitution.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A condition of extreme poverty where someone lacks basic necessities.

examples.text: The prolonged economic depression plunged many families into deep penury.
He spent his youth in penury before finding success as an author.
Charitable organizations work tirelessly to alleviate widespread penury.
The once proud estate fell into utter ruin and penury.

distractors.lemma: The act of writing with a fountain pen.
A severe restriction on public movement.
An enclosure used for keeping farm animals.
The quality of being overly cautious with money.
A strong desire to acquire luxury items.

mnemonics: Penury sounds like penniless, meaning having no money at all.

senses.definition: Tending to betray; especially having a treacherous character as attributed to the Carthaginians by the Romans.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unfaithful and deceptive, often breaking trust in a sneaky way.

examples.text: His perfidious actions ultimately destroyed the fragile alliance.
History judges the general as a perfidious commander who abandoned his troops.
She could not forgive her business partner for his perfidious betrayal.
The spy engaged in perfidious behavior throughout the negotiations.
The perfidious Judas

distractors.lemma: Showing an extreme dislike for perfumed scents.
Acting in a manner that is excessively polite.
Tending to move at a very slow pace.
Displaying a complete lack of emotional expression.
Characterized by loud and boastful declarations.

mnemonics: Perfidious contains the sound of perfidy, which is the act of betraying trust.

senses.definition: Hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done quickly and carelessly without paying attention to important details.

examples.text: The inspector gave the machinery a perfunctory glance before signing off.
She offered a perfunctory apology and rushed out of the room.
His perfunctory review of the manuscript missed several major errors.
They performed their duties with a perfunctory attitude that lacked enthusiasm.
Perfunctory courtesy

distractors.lemma: Relating to the performance of musical instruments.
Extremely thorough and detailed in nature.
Marked by an excess of formal ceremony.
Requiring intense physical exertion.
Occurring at regular and predictable intervals.

senses.definition: Done or produced as a formality only.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Done simply as a routine duty or formality without real care.

examples.text: He gave a perfunctory nod to the audience as he took the stage.
The handshake between the rivals was entirely perfunctory.
She completed the mandatory paperwork with a perfunctory wave of her hand.
Their polite greetings were merely perfunctory gestures.

distractors.lemma: Pertaining to the function of mechanical parts.
Carried out with deep emotional involvement.
Created through a complex artistic process.
Designed to provoke a strong public reaction.
Involving a high degree of personal risk.

mnemonics: Perfunctory sounds like performing a chore just to get it done quickly.

senses.definition: Exceedingly harmful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely harmful or destructive to people or things.

examples.text: Pollution has a pernicious effect on local marine life.
The dictator spread pernicious propaganda throughout the nation.
Doctors warned the public about the pernicious nature of the new virus.
Rumors can have a pernicious influence on a community.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the bones or skeletal structure.
Characterized by excessive speed and agility.
Beneficial to overall health and well-being.
Showing a high level of artistic skill.
Pertaining to financial investments.

senses.definition: Working or spreading in a hidden and usually injurious way.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Spreading harm in a quiet, secret, and dangerous way.

examples.text: A pernicious disease slowly weakened his immune system over the years.
The corrupt official exercised a pernicious influence over the department.
Subtle prejudices can be just as pernicious as overt discrimination.
The mold caused pernicious damage to the structure of the house.

distractors.lemma: Operating in plain sight for everyone to observe.
Moving swiftly across an open landscape.
Generating bright flashes of light.
Providing essential nutrients for growth.
Displaying a cheerful and outgoing personality.

mnemonics: Pernicious starts with per, like poison that causes destruction.

senses.definition: Acutely insightful and wise.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having great wisdom and the ability to understand things clearly.

examples.text: The perspicacious investor anticipated the market crash before anyone else.
Her perspicacious analysis of the novel impressed her literature professor.
An astute and perspicacious leader can navigate any crisis.
He made several perspicacious observations during the debate.
Much too perspicacious to be taken in by such a spurious argument

distractors.lemma: Lacking the ability to see clearly in the dark.
Prone to making hasty and foolish decisions.
Displaying an unusual fear of open spaces.
Related to the study of ancient perspectives.
Suffering from a lack of focus and attention.

senses.definition: Mentally acute or penetratingly discerning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Quick to notice and understand complicated situations.

examples.text: The detective made a perspicacious deduction that solved the mystery.
With perspicacious judgment, she chose the winning strategy.
His perspicacious mind allowed him to master complex subjects quickly.
She offered a perspicacious critique of the proposed policy.
Much too perspicacious to be taken in by so spurious an argument

distractors.lemma: Involving heavy physical labor and endurance.
Characterized by dullness and lack of imagination.
Relating to the physical structure of the eye.
Prone to frequent misunderstandings.
Marked by an absence of logical thought.

mnemonics: Perspicacious has perspective inside it, meaning seeing things clearly.

senses.definition: Spreading or spread throughout.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Spreading widely throughout an area or a group of people.

examples.text: The pervasive scent of pine filled every corner of the rustic cabin.
A pervasive sense of anxiety settled over the kingdom as the rumor spread.
Engineers worked tirelessly to eliminate the pervasive static from the radio transmission.
Her pervasive influence can be seen in every single department of the academy.
The pervasive odor of garlic
An error is pervasive if it is material to more than one conclusion

distractors.lemma: Acting in a secretive and covert manner.
Relating to a medical operation or surgical procedure.
Marked by extreme poverty and destitution.
Possessing a sharp and biting flavor.

mnemonics: PER VAded All SActivites: it spread everywhere.

senses.definition: Easily irritated or annoyed.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Behaving like a grumpy child who gets annoyed very easily.

examples.text: The petulant toddler threw his wooden spoon across the kitchen floor.
She grew petulant when the librarian asked her to lower her voice.
His petulant refusal to cooperate derailed the entire diplomatic meeting.
Even a minor critique would make the young actor look petulant.

distractors.lemma: Showing great courage in the face of danger.
Relating to the cultivation of flowering plants.
Eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight.
Extremely small in size or importance.

mnemonics: PETulant pets get easily annoyed.

senses.definition: A wooden instrument of punishment on a post with holes for the wrists and neck; offenders were locked in and so exposed to public scorn.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: An old wooden device used for locking up wrongdoers so people could mock them.

examples.text: The village criminal was locked in the pillory for a full afternoon.
Townspeople gathered in the square to throw rotten fruit at the man in the pillory.
Historians examined the ancient pillory preserved in the museum basement.
Being placed in the pillory was considered a fate worse than physical lashes.

distractors.lemma: A tall stone column used for astronomical observation.
A heavy iron gate that seals the entrance of a castle.
A decorative pillar placed at the corner of a grand estate.
A large woven basket used for harvesting autumn grapes.

mnemonics: A PILLORY makes you ill and sorry in public.

senses.definition: Concise and full of meaning.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Brief, powerful, and full of substance.

examples.text: The CEO delivered a pithy remark that captured the entire strategy in one sentence.
Scholars admire the philosopher for his pithy essays on morality.
Her pithy response ended the debate before it could drag on.
He offered a pithy summary of the lengthy historical text.
Welcomed her pithy comments

distractors.lemma: Lacking any nutritional value or substance.
Covered in a sticky, resinous substance.
Extremely long and tedious in presentation.
Filled with doubt and uncertainty.

mnemonics: PITHY sounds like pith, the core of the fruit: short and deep.

senses.definition: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To make someone less angry or hostile by being nice to them.

examples.text: The diplomat attempted to placate the hostile crowd with promises of reform.
She tried to placate her crying infant with a soft lullaby.
Management offered concessions to placate the striking workers.
Nothing could placate the furious merchant after the theft.

distractors.lemma: To make a situation significantly worse or more violent.
To place an object in a specific geographic location.
To cleanse thoroughly using chemical detergents.
To confuse someone with difficult riddles.

mnemonics: PLACAte sounds like plate: offer a peace offering on a plate to calm someone.

senses.definition: A trite or obvious remark.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A boring, overused remark that offers no new ideas.

examples.text: His speech was filled with every political platitude imaginable.
Instead of offering real help, she offered a useless platitude.
The editorial was dismissed as a collection of tired platitudes.
We grew weary of hearing the same empty platitude over and over.

distractors.lemma: A flat geographical region devoid of mountains.
A musical instrument resembling a small lute.
A precious metal alloy used in fine jewelry.
A formal agreement signed by multiple nations.

mnemonics: FLATitude leads to a boring PLATITUDE.

senses.definition: Extreme excess.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A huge, excessive amount of something.

examples.text: The banquet featured a plethora of rich dishes from around the world.
She faced a plethora of choices when selecting her university courses.
Despite the plethora of evidence, the jury remained undecided.
The library possesses a plethora of rare manuscripts.

distractors.lemma: A complete lack of resources or supplies.
A medical condition causing severe joint inflammation.
A complex mathematical equation with multiple variables.
A dangerous journey across uncharted waters.

mnemonics: PLEthora sounds like plethora of pleasant things: too many to count.

senses.definition: A writer who argues in opposition to others (especially in theology).
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A person who writes fierce arguments attacking the opinions of others.

examples.text: The famous polemic spared no opponent in his latest theological tract.
As a relentless polemic, he constantly challenged established church doctrines.
The university invited a noted polemic to speak on religious philosophy.
History remembers him as a brilliant polemic rather than a gentle scholar.

distractors.lemma: A long wooden pole used for navigating shallow rivers.
A specialist in the cultivation of polar bear habitats.
An astronomer who maps distant celestial bodies.
A craftsman who builds traditional wooden sailing ships.

senses.definition: A controversy (especially over a belief or dogma).
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A fierce written or verbal attack on someone else's opinions or beliefs.

examples.text: The professor published a sharp polemic against contemporary literary theory.
Her latest essay is a brilliant polemic that challenges traditional economic dogma.
Critics praised the author for writing such a fierce polemic on modern politics.
Instead of a balanced analysis, the journalist delivered a scathing polemic.

distractors.lemma: A long journey undertaken by foot across difficult terrain.
An ornamental structure placed at the center of a public garden.
The magnetic attraction between opposite poles of a magnet.
A polished finish applied to metal surfaces before assembly.

mnemonics: POLEmic: someone who likes to poke the bear with arguments.

senses.definition: Slow and laborious because of weight.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Moving heavily and with great effort due to physical weight.

examples.text: The hiker made slow progress across the mud with his ponderous boots.
Workers struggled to move the ponderous crates into the warehouse.
The knight found his armor increasingly ponderous during the long march.
Elephants move with a ponderous grace across the dry savannah.
Ponderous prehistoric beasts
A ponderous yawn

distractors.lemma: Deeply thoughtful and inclined to serious philosophical contemplation.
Extremely bright and shining with a brilliant luster.
Quickly changing position without warning or stability.
Marked by extreme poverty and lack of basic resources.

senses.definition: Having great mass and weight and unwieldiness.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely heavy, bulky, and difficult to manage.

examples.text: They discarded the ponderous wooden desk because it blocked the hallway.
The sculpture was a ponderous block of marble that required a crane to lift.
Navigating the ponderous machinery through the narrow doors was nearly impossible.
He struggled under the weight of the ponderous iron shield.
A ponderous stone
A ponderous burden

distractors.lemma: Possessing a sweet and pleasant fragrance like spring flowers.
Capable of floating easily on the surface of deep water.
Exhibiting great speed and agility in tight spaces.
Transparent and clear enough to see through completely.

senses.definition: Labored and dull.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Dull, tedious, and lacking any lively spirit.

examples.text: The lecture was so ponderous that half the audience fell asleep.
She suffered through a ponderous speech before the main event began.
His writing style is often described as overly academic and ponderous.
The committee meeting dragged on with ponderous discussions about minor paperwork.
A ponderous speech

distractors.lemma: Sharp and biting in style, causing immediate discomfort.
Full of excitement and vibrant theatrical energy.
Extremely brief and concise in expression.
Richly decorated with ornate patterns and bright colors.

mnemonics: Ponderous sounds like ponder plus ous, meaning you are thinking deeply while carrying a heavy load that slows you down.

senses.definition: Concerned with practical matters.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Focused on practical solutions and real-world results rather than theory.

examples.text: She took a pragmatic approach to solving the budget crisis.
Engineers need to remain pragmatic when designing bridges for harsh climates.
His pragmatic decision saved the company from bankruptcy.
Instead of arguing about ideals, they offered pragmatic steps forward.
A matter-of-fact (or pragmatic) approach to the problem

distractors.lemma: Obsessed with strict adherence to ancient religious dogma.
Prone to dramatic emotional outbursts in public.
Excessively focused on grammar and linguistic purity.
Inclined to believe in magical remedies and superstition.

senses.definition: Of or concerning the theory of pragmatism.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Relating to the philosophical system that evaluates theories by their practical consequences.

examples.text: The professor lectured on pragmatic philosophy and its impact on modern education.
William James is famous for developing pragmatic theories of truth.
Her thesis explored the pragmatic framework established in the early twentieth century.
The seminar contrasted idealist metaphysics with pragmatic analysis.

distractors.lemma: Relating to the study of ancient fossils and prehistoric life.
Derived from strict mathematical formulas and geometry.
Pertaining to the psychological study of dreams and sleep.
Rooted in romantic poetry and the appreciation of nature.

senses.definition: Guided by practical experience and observation rather than theory.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Based on hands-on experience and actual observation instead of abstract ideas.

examples.text: Experienced mechanics use a pragmatic method to diagnose engine failure.
The director made a pragmatic choice based on years of working in the field.
Farmers often take a pragmatic view of weather patterns.
Her pragmatic assessment of the market came from decades of trading.
Not ideology but pragmatic politics

distractors.lemma: Imagined entirely through creative artistic visualization.
Derived from unverified rumors spread by local villagers.
Calculated using advanced theoretical physics models.
Based on idealistic dreams of a utopian society.

mnemonics: Pragmatic sounds like practicalmatic, reminding you that it is all about practical results.

senses.definition: Idle or foolish and irrelevant talk.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Silly, meaningless chatter that goes on and on.

examples.text: I grew tired of the endless prattle at the party and went home early.
The children filled the backyard with joyful prattle while playing games.
She ignored the political prattle on television and read a book instead.
His speech was mostly foolish prattle with very few facts.

distractors.lemma: A metal instrument used for measuring atmospheric pressure.
A minor legal document used to transfer property ownership.
The rhythmic beating of a drum during a ceremony.
A delicate pattern woven into fine silk fabric.

mnemonics: Prattle sounds like rattle, as in a baby's rattle making endless meaningless noise.

senses.definition: A precipitated solid substance in suspension or after settling or filtering.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A solid that forms and falls to the bottom of a liquid during a chemical reaction.

examples.text: The chemist carefully filtered the red precipitate from the liquid solution.
After the reagent was added, a heavy precipitate formed at the bottom of the flask.
They collected the fine precipitate to measure its mass on the scale.
The unwanted precipitate was washed away with distilled water.

distractors.lemma: A sudden drop in temperature caused by atmospheric pressure.
The act of falling steeply from a high elevation.
A written order for medication issued by a physician.
An introductory statement preceding a formal document.

mnemonics: Think of precipitation like rain or snow falling down from the sky as solid particles drop to the bottom.

senses.definition: Keep from happening or arising; make impossible.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To prevent something from happening before it can even start.

examples.text: Signing the non-disclosure agreement will preclude any future leaks of company secrets.
His lack of formal qualifications tends to preclude him from high-ranking diplomatic positions.
Strict security protocols preclude unauthorized personnel from entering the laboratory.
Bad weather might preclude the spacecraft from launching on schedule.
Your role in the projects precludes your involvement in the competitive project

distractors.lemma: To include multiple subjects within a single curriculum.
To conclude an argument with a definitive statement.
To decrease in volume or intensity over time.
To promote an ongoing negotiation process.

senses.definition: Make impossible, especially beforehand.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To block or stop something in advance so it cannot happen.

examples.text: Early intervention can preclude the onset of chronic health conditions.
The new regulations effectively preclude any possibility of unfair market manipulation.
Taking precautions beforehand helps preclude potential accidents on the factory floor.
Her prior commitments preclude her from attending the board meeting tomorrow.

distractors.lemma: To include additional clauses in a legal contract.
To increase the speed of a chemical reaction.
To persuade someone to change their mind.
To predict future events based on past data.

mnemonics: Preclude sounds like pre-close, meaning you close the door on something before it happens.

senses.definition: Characterized by or characteristic of exceptionally early development or maturity (especially in mental aptitude).
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Showing unusually advanced mental talent or maturity at a very young age.

examples.text: The precocious child astonished her piano teachers by mastering complex sonatas at age four.
His precocious grasp of quantum physics baffled university researchers.
Known for her precocious intellect, she entered college before her teenage years.
The precocious author published her first bestselling novel while still in middle school.
A precocious child
A precocious achievement

distractors.lemma: Showing signs of extreme caution and hesitation.
Characterized by a persistent lack of focus.
Displaying anger and resentment toward authority.
Exhibiting physical traits typical of old age.

senses.definition: Appearing or developing early.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Appearing or developing much earlier than usual.

examples.text: Botanists noted the precocious blooming of the cherry trees during an unusually warm winter.
The orchard yielded a precocious harvest of apples weeks ahead of schedule.
Birds showing precocious migration patterns left the sanctuary before autumn began.
Their precocious interest in architecture was evident when they built detailed models as toddlers.
Precocious flowers appear before the leaves as in some species of magnolias

distractors.lemma: Delayed in growth due to poor nutrition.
Existing in a state of suspended animation.
Proceeding at a very slow and steady pace.
Occurring exclusively during the night hours.

mnemonics: Pre-cocious sounds like pre-cook, meaning someone whose mind is cooked and ready early.

senses.definition: A predisposition in favor of something.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A natural preference or bias toward a specific thing.

examples.text: Her clear predilection for classical literature influenced her choice of university major.
He has a lifelong predilection for spicy food and exotic spices.
The curator noted a strong predilection among collectors for abstract expressionism.
My predilection for quiet solitude makes rural living very appealing.
A predilection for expensive cars

distractors.lemma: A strict adherence to traditional rules and customs.
An ongoing dispute between neighboring nations.
A medical condition affecting joint mobility.
A formal prediction about future weather patterns.

senses.definition: A strong liking.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A deep fondness or preference for something.

examples.text: She confessed her secret predilection for late-night horror movies.
His predilection for fast cars led him to spend his weekends at the racetrack.
They share a mutual predilection for hiking in remote mountain ranges.
The chef demonstrated a clear predilection for fresh Mediterranean herbs.

distractors.lemma: A severe dislike of public speaking.
An inability to make simple decisions.
A temporary loss of memory.
A financial obligation that must be paid.

mnemonics: Pre-election means you already lean toward a certain candidate before voting.

senses.definition: Perceiving the significance of events before they occur.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Having the ability to know or sense what will happen in the future.

examples.text: Her prescient warning about the economic crash saved investors millions of dollars.
The author wrote a prescient novel that predicted modern digital surveillance decades in advance.
Investors admired his prescient ability to back winning technology startups early on.
The historian offered a prescient analysis of the shifting geopolitical landscape.
Extraordinarily prescient memoranda on the probable course of postwar relations

distractors.lemma: Lacking awareness of immediate surroundings.
Possessing extensive knowledge of ancient history.
Acting impulsively without considering consequences.
Prone to making careless mistakes in calculation.

mnemonics: Pre means before, and science or scire means to know, so you know things before they happen.

senses.definition: Be deliberately ambiguous or unclear in order to mislead or withhold information.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: To speak evasively in order to hide the truth.

examples.text: When asked about the missing funds, the director chose to prevaricate rather than give a direct answer.
Politicians often prevaricate during debates to avoid taking an unpopular stance.
Instead of answering my question honestly, he continued to prevaricate for several minutes.
Do not prevaricate when the police officer asks you for your account of the accident.

distractors.lemma: Prepare carefully for an upcoming event or formal meeting.
Prevent someone from entering a restricted area without permission.
Provide a detailed explanation of a complex scientific theory.
Promote a product aggressively through deceptive advertising.
Process legal documents with unnecessary bureaucratic delay.

mnemonics: Pre-var-icate sounds like pre-fabricate, meaning making up a fake story.

senses.definition: Completely free from dirt or contamination.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Completely pure and untouched by dirt or pollution.

examples.text: The divers discovered a pristine coral reef untouched by human activity.
After the heavy snowfall, the landscape looked entirely pristine and quiet.
She keeps her vintage sports car in pristine condition.
The mountain stream was so clear and pristine that we drank directly from it.
Pristine mountain snow

distractors.lemma: Showing signs of advanced age and physical decay.
Prone to sudden emotional outbursts under pressure.
Painted with bright colors to attract attention.
Prepared meticulously for a long journey.
Pertaining to ancient historical artifacts.

senses.definition: Immaculately clean and unused.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: In its original condition and completely unused.

examples.text: He found a first edition of the novel in pristine condition inside the attic.
The museum exhibited a sword kept in pristine armor cases for centuries.
Even though it was manufactured decades ago, the machine remains pristine.
She wore a pristine white dress to the graduation ceremony.
Handed her his pristine white handkerchief

distractors.lemma: Designed for maximum efficiency and modern comfort.
Damaged severely by continuous exposure to moisture.
Decorated with elaborate patterns and precious stones.
Discarded carelessly after a single use.
Derived from recycled synthetic materials.

mnemonics: Pristine sounds like priest-clean, extremely pure.

senses.definition: Complete and confirmed integrity; having strong moral principles.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Unquestionable honesty and strong moral character.

examples.text: The judge was a woman of unquestioned probity and fairness.
His reputation for probity made him the ideal candidate for the ethics committee.
She conducted her financial affairs with absolute probity.
The journalist questioned the probity of the corporate executives.
In a world where financial probity may not be widespread
He enjoys an exaggerated reputation for probity

distractors.lemma: A strong desire to achieve wealth and social status.
The quality of being overly cautious in financial matters.
An intense curiosity about scientific phenomena.
A tendency to act impulsively without foresight.
The ability to solve complex mathematical equations.

mnemonics: Probity sounds like probe-integrity, digging deep for honesty.

senses.definition: A natural inclination.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: A natural tendency or preference for something.

examples.text: His artistic proclivity became apparent when he started sketching on every surface.
She has a natural proclivity for languages and learns them quickly.
The historian noted a proclivity among monarchs for grand architecture.
Despite his scientific training, he always retained a proclivity for fiction.
He has a proclivity for exaggeration

distractors.lemma: A sudden decline in physical health or stamina.
The process of climbing steep mountain terrain.
A formal declaration of independence from a group.
The legal right to inherit family property.
A strong aversion to modern technology.

mnemonics: Proclivity sounds like pro-cliff-activity, leaning toward the edge naturally.

senses.definition: Recklessly wasteful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Spending money or resources in a reckless and wasteful way.

examples.text: His prodigal spending habits eventually led to bankruptcy.
The billionaire lived a prodigal lifestyle, purchasing mansions he never visited.
She regretted her prodigal purchases at the designer boutique.
The empire fell because of the prodigal use of its treasury on luxuries.
Prodigal in their expenditures

distractors.lemma: Productive and yielding a high harvest each season.
Prudent in saving money for future emergencies.
Proud and arrogant in social interactions.
Profound in philosophical thought and reasoning.
Proactive in solving community problems.

mnemonics: Prodigal sounds like prod-to-gale, blowing money away like the wind.

senses.definition: Recklessly wasteful.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Extremely wasteful with resources or money.

examples.text: The emperor's profligate spending bankrupted the entire nation.
Critics condemned the corporation for its profligate use of natural resources.
He inherited a fortune and quickly exhausted it through profligate habits.
Her profligate lifestyle left her with massive debts by age thirty.

distractors.lemma: Profitable and generating steady commercial revenue.
Profoundly knowledgeable about classical literature.
Progressive in political and social reforms.
Protected by legal agreements and patents.
Prohibited by strict government regulations.

senses.definition: Unrestrained by convention or morality.
senses.plainLanguageDefinition: Living in a way that ignores all moral rules and social standards.
